a: He did not want to travel around Judea
p: A few early witnesses say Jesus "did not have authority" to walk in Judea.

readings.w: Nearly all Greek manuscripts, including Papyrus 66 and 75 (about 175–225), Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: οὐ γὰρ ἤθελεν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ περιπατεῖν
readings.en: for he did not want to walk in Judea
readings.plain: He did not want to travel around Judea

readings.w: Codex Washingtonianus (W, 400s), some Old Latin manuscripts, the Old Syriac (Curetonian), Chrysostom, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: οὐ γὰρ εἶχεν ἐξουσίαν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ περιπατεῖν
readings.en: for he did not have authority (freedom) to walk in Judea
readings.plain: He did not have the freedom to travel around Judea

why: "Did not want" has overwhelming support. "Did not have authority" probably arose to explain why Jesus stayed away, or as a loose rendering in a version.

a: I am not going up to this festival
p: Many manuscripts and the KJV's Greek say "not yet," which removes the seeming contradiction with 7:10.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s), Bezae (400s), the Latin Vulgate and most Old Latin, the Old Syriac, the Bohairic Coptic, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT
readings.orig: ἐγὼ οὐκ ἀναβαίνω εἰς τὴν ἑορτὴν ταύτην
readings.en: I am not going up to this festival
readings.plain: I am not going up to this festival

readings.w: Papyrus 66 and 75 (about 175–225), Codex Vaticanus (300s), W, the Byzantine majority, as reported by Metzger; THGNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "I go not up yet")
readings.orig: ἐγὼ οὔπω ἀναβαίνω εἰς τὴν ἑορτὴν ταύτην
readings.en: I am not yet going up to this festival
readings.plain: I am not yet going up to this festival

why: "Not yet" has the two early papyri and Vaticanus, and the Tyndale House edition follows it. But "not" is the harder reading: it is easy to see why a copyist would change "not" to "not yet" to protect Jesus from seeming to change his mind (the very charge Porphyry later made, as Jerome reports), and hard to see why anyone would change "not yet" to "not." The "yet" may also have come in from "not yet" at the end of the verse.
b: This is a real split among modern editions: NA28 and SBL print "not," THGNT prints "not yet." English versions print "not" with a footnote (ESV, NIV, NRSV) or "not yet" (KJV, NKJV, and the 1984 NIV).

a: this man is the Messiah
p: Later manuscripts add a second "truly," behind the KJV's "the very Christ."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ χριστός
readings.en: that this is the Messiah
readings.plain: this man is the Messiah

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "this is the very Christ")
readings.orig: ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὁ χριστός
readings.en: that this is truly the Messiah
readings.plain: this man is truly the Messiah

why: The second "truly" is missing from the oldest manuscripts and looks like an emphasis added by copyists. It does not change the meaning.

a: For the Spirit had not yet come
t: "The Spirit" or "the Holy Spirit was not yet given"?
p: Copyists filled out John's bare "the Spirit was not yet" with "Holy" or "given."

readings.w: Papyrus 75, Papyrus 66 (corrected), Sinaiticus, Θ and others, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT
readings.orig: οὔπω γὰρ ἦν πνεῦμα
readings.en: for the Spirit was not yet
readings.plain: For the Spirit had not yet come

readings.w: Papyrus 66 (first hand), L, W, Ψ and the Byzantine majority, as reported by Metzger; THGNT (as the Tyndale House edition data in TAGNT shows), Textus Receptus (KJV "the Holy Ghost was not yet given," with "given" in italics)
readings.orig: οὔπω γὰρ ἦν πνεῦμα ἅγιον
readings.en: for the Holy Spirit was not yet
readings.plain: For the Holy Spirit had not yet come

readings.w: Most Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, the Syriac, Eusebius, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: οὔπω γὰρ ἦν πνεῦμα δεδομένον
readings.en: for the Spirit was not yet given
readings.plain: For the Spirit had not yet been given

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s) and a few others, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: οὔπω γὰρ ἦν πνεῦμα ἅγιον δεδομένον
readings.en: for the Holy Spirit was not yet given
readings.plain: For the Holy Spirit had not yet been given

why: The short form is the hardest, and the others can all be explained as attempts to soften it, since copyists did not want John to seem to say the Spirit did not exist. NA28 and SBL print it. The Tyndale House edition departs from them here and prints "Holy Spirit," with the Byzantine text; the meaning is the same. Nearly all English versions add "given" in translation anyway.

a: Some in the crowd
p: The KJV says "Many of the people," from the Byzantine text. The older text just says "some from the crowd."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ἐκ τοῦ ὄχλου οὖν ἀκούσαντες τῶν λόγων τούτων
readings.en: so some from the crowd, having heard these words
readings.plain: Some in the crowd

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "Many of the people therefore, when they heard this saying")
readings.orig: πολλοὶ οὖν ἐκ τοῦ ὄχλου ἀκούσαντες τὸν λόγον
readings.en: so many from the crowd, having heard the saying
readings.plain: Many in the crowd

why: The Greek "from the crowd" can stand for "some of the crowd" without a word for "some." "Many" looks like a copyist's way of supplying the missing subject. The meaning hardly changes.

a: Never has any man spoken in this way!
p: Later manuscripts lengthen the officers' answer, as in the KJV's "Never man spake like this man."

readings.w: Papyrus 66 (corrected) and 75, Vaticanus, L, T, W, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: Οὐδέποτε ἐλάλησεν οὕτως ἄνθρωπος
readings.en: never did a man speak this way
readings.plain: Never has any man spoken in this way!

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV), as reported by Metzger; longer forms also in Papyrus 66 (first hand), Sinaiticus (first hand) and Bezae
readings.orig: Οὐδέποτε οὕτως ἐλάλησεν ἄνθρωπος, ὡς οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος
readings.en: never did a man speak like this man
readings.plain: Never has any man spoken the way this man speaks!

why: The shorter text is older and widely attested; the longer forms vary in wording, which suggests they were added to complete the comparison.

a: at an earlier time
p: The KJV says Nicodemus "came to Jesus by night," from the Byzantine text, recalling 3:2.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ὁ ἐλθὼν πρὸς αὐτὸν [τὸ] πρότερον
readings.en: the one who came to him before
readings.plain: at an earlier time

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "he that came to Jesus by night")
readings.orig: ὁ ἐλθὼν νυκτὸς πρὸς αὐτόν
readings.en: the one who came to him by night
readings.plain: at night

why: "Before" has the older support. "By night" was likely added from 3:2 and 19:39; some manuscripts combine both. Metzger reports that Codex Sinaiticus (first hand) leaves out the whole clause.

a: no prophet is raised up
p: Papyrus 66 reads "the Prophet does not arise from Galilee," which makes the rulers' claim accurate.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας προφήτης οὐκ ἐγείρεται
readings.en: out of Galilee a prophet does not arise
readings.plain: no prophet is raised up

readings.w: Papyrus 66 (first hand, about AD 200), as reported in Comfort and in the NA28 apparatus
readings.orig: ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας ὁ προφήτης οὐκ ἐγείρεται
readings.en: out of Galilee the Prophet does not arise
readings.plain: the Prophet is not raised up

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: προφήτης ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας οὐκ ἐγήγερται
readings.en: no prophet has arisen out of Galilee
readings.plain: no prophet has been raised up

why: Almost every manuscript lacks the article. The reading of Papyrus 66 is attractive, since it ties back to "the Prophet" in 7:40 and avoids the problem of Jonah, but it has almost no support and may be a correction for exactly that reason. The Byzantine perfect tense ("has arisen") does not change the sense; the KJV translates it as "ariseth."

a: Then they went away, each one to his own home.
t: The story of the adulterous woman (7:53–8:11)
p: The oldest manuscripts go straight from 7:52 to 8:12. This reading covers the whole passage, 7:53–8:11.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D, 400s), most later Greek manuscripts, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV); most Old Latin manuscripts and the Vulgate; known to Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine, as reported by Metzger. NA28 prints it in double brackets as a later addition; SBLGNT and THGNT leave it out of the text and give it in the apparatus
readings.orig: Καὶ ἐπορεύθησαν ἕκαστος εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and each went to his own house
readings.plain: Then they went away, each one to his own home.

readings.w: Papyrus 66 (about 200) and 75 (about 175–225), Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), W, Θ, Ψ, L and Δ (which leave a blank space), Alexandrinus and Ephraemi (pages lost here, but too short to have held it), the Old Syriac and the Sahidic Coptic, as reported by Metzger; no Greek church writer comments on it before Euthymius Zigabenus in the 1100s
readings.orig: (7:53–8:11 absent; 7:52 is followed by 8:12)
readings.en: the passage is not there

readings.w: Family 13 manuscripts (the Ferrar group), as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: (placed after Luke 21:38)
readings.en: the story stands in Luke, after Jesus teaching daily in the temple

readings.w: Family 1 manuscripts and some others, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: (placed after John 21:25, at the end of the Gospel)
readings.en: the story stands as an appendix to John

why: The Plain prints the passage in its familiar place, as nearly all Bibles do, under a heading that says it is a later addition. The evidence that it was not part of John's original text is very strong: it is missing in all the earliest manuscripts and versions from every region, it moves around (after John 7:36, 7:44, 21:25 or Luke 21:38), many manuscripts that have it mark it with signs of doubt, and its vocabulary is unlike John's. Yet the story itself is old: a story of Jesus and a woman accused of many sins was known to Papias (as Eusebius reports) and is told in the Didascalia from the 200s. Most scholars think it is a true tradition about Jesus that circulated on its own and was later placed here.
b: Switching to the second reading hides only 7:53; the rest of the passage, 8:1–11, goes with it. Each later verse of the story has its own smaller variants, listed at those verses.

a: began to write in the dirt with his finger
t: "As though he did not hear them"
p: The KJV adds that Jesus wrote "as though he heard them not," from the Byzantine text.

readings.w: NA28 text of the passage, following the older manuscripts that contain the story
readings.orig: κάτω κύψας τῷ δακτύλῳ κατέγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν
readings.en: stooping down, he wrote with his finger on the ground
readings.plain: began to write in the dirt with his finger

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "as though he heard them not")
readings.orig: κάτω κύψας τῷ δακτύλῳ ἔγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν, μὴ προσποιούμενος
readings.en: stooping down, he wrote with his finger on the ground, not pretending (to hear)
readings.plain: began to write in the dirt with his finger, as though he did not hear them

why: The phrase is missing in the earliest copies of the story and looks like an explanation of why Jesus wrote. A few later manuscripts add in 8:8 that he wrote "the sins of each one of them," which is also an explanation.

a: When they heard this, they began to leave, one after another, starting with the elders.
p: The KJV adds that they were "convicted by their own conscience" and left "even unto the last."

readings.w: NA28 text of the passage, following the older manuscripts that contain the story
readings.orig: οἱ δὲ ἀκούσαντες ἐξήρχοντο εἷς καθ᾽ εἷς ἀρξάμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων
readings.en: they, having heard, went out one by one, beginning with the elders
readings.plain: When they heard this, they began to leave, one after another, starting with the elders.

readings.w: Byzantine majority and Textus Receptus ("convicted by their conscience"); the Textus Receptus alone also has "to the last" (KJV)
readings.orig: οἱ δὲ ἀκούσαντες, καὶ ὑπὸ τῆς συνειδήσεως ἐλεγχόμενοι, ἐξήρχοντο εἷς καθ᾽ εἷς, ἀρξάμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων ἕως τῶν ἐσχάτων
readings.en: they, having heard and being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning with the elders, to the last
readings.plain: When they heard this, they were convicted by their own conscience, and they began to leave, one after another, starting with the elders, down to the last one.

why: The added phrases explain what the shorter text leaves to the reader and are not in the earlier copies of the story.

a: Jesus stood up straight and said to her, "Woman, where are they?
p: The KJV's Greek adds that Jesus "saw none but the woman" and asked where "those thine accusers" were.

readings.w: NA28 text of the passage, following the older manuscripts that contain the story
readings.orig: ἀνακύψας δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν αὐτῇ· Γύναι, ποῦ εἰσιν;
readings.en: Jesus, standing up, said to her, 'Woman, where are they?'
readings.plain: Jesus stood up straight and said to her, "Woman, where are they?

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἀνακύψας δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ μηδένα θεασάμενος πλὴν τῆς γυναικός, εἶπεν αὐτῇ, Ἡ γυνή, ποῦ εἰσιν ἐκεῖνοι οἱ κατήγοροί σου;
readings.en: Jesus, standing up and seeing no one but the woman, said to her, 'Woman, where are those accusers of yours?'
readings.plain: Jesus stood up straight and saw no one but the woman. He said to her, "Woman, where are those accusers of yours?

why: The longer text fills in details. The shorter form is followed by NA28 and most modern versions; the story's text varies more than any other passage in the Gospels, a sign of its separate life.

a: I do not condemn you either. Go, and from now on, do not keep on sinning.
p: The KJV's "go, and sin no more" lacks "from now on." Most Byzantine manuscripts also have "judge" for "condemn."

readings.w: NA28 text of the passage, following the older manuscripts that contain the story
readings.orig: οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου, [καὶ] ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε
readings.en: neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more
readings.plain: I do not condemn you either. Go, and from now on, do not keep on sinning.

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more")
readings.orig: οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου καὶ μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε
readings.en: neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more
readings.plain: I do not condemn you either. Go, and do not keep on sinning.

readings.w: Byzantine majority
readings.orig: οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κρίνω· πορεύου καὶ μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε
readings.en: neither do I judge you; go and sin no more
readings.plain: I do not judge you either. Go, and do not keep on sinning.

why: "From now on" is in the form of the story printed by NA28. It adds emphasis but not a new meaning. "Judge" in the Byzantine text is a weaker word than "condemn," but the sense of Jesus' answer is the same.

a: It is I together with the Father who sent me.
t: "The Father who sent me" or "the one who sent me"?
p: A few early witnesses lack "the Father," giving "I and the one who sent me."

readings.w: Papyrus 66 and 75, Vaticanus, W, most manuscripts, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: ἀλλ᾽ ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πέμψας με πατήρ
readings.en: but I and the Father who sent me
readings.plain: It is I together with the Father who sent me.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Bezae, the Old Syriac, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: ἀλλ᾽ ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πέμψας με
readings.en: but I and the one who sent me
readings.plain: It is I together with the one who sent me.

why: "The Father" has strong early support. The shorter form matches John's common phrase "the one who sent me" and may be a copyist's slip into the familiar wording.

a: Why am I even talking to you?
p: The earliest copy of John, Papyrus 66, adds "I told you," which turns Jesus' answer into a statement.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: Τὴν ἀρχὴν ὅ τι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν
readings.en: (as for) the beginning, what I am even saying to you
readings.plain: Why am I even talking to you?

readings.w: Papyrus 66 (first hand, about 200), as reported by Metzger and by Comfort
readings.orig: Εἶπον ὑμῖν τὴν ἀρχὴν ὅ τι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν
readings.en: I told you at the beginning what I am also telling you
readings.plain: I told you at the beginning what I am telling you now.

why: The added "I told you" looks like a copyist's attempt to make sense of a very hard sentence. No other early witness has it. It shows how one early reader understood the words: as a claim about what Jesus had said from the start.

a: I speak of the things I have seen at the Father's side. You, in the same way, do the things you heard from your father.
t: "Heard from the father" or "seen with your father"?
p: The Byzantine text adds "my" and "your" and has "seen" twice, which makes the contrast of two fathers explicit.

readings.w: Papyrus 66 and 75, Vaticanus, W and others, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ἃ ἐγὼ ἑώρακα παρὰ τῷ πατρὶ λαλῶ· καὶ ὑμεῖς οὖν ἃ ἠκούσατε παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ποιεῖτε
readings.en: what I have seen with the Father I speak; and you then do what you heard from the father
readings.plain: I speak of the things I have seen at the Father's side. You, in the same way, do the things you heard from your father.

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "I speak that which I have seen with my Father: and ye do that which ye have seen with your father")
readings.orig: ἐγὼ ὃ ἑώρακα παρὰ τῷ πατρί μου, λαλῶ· καὶ ὑμεῖς οὖν ὃ ἑωράκατε παρὰ τῷ πατρὶ ὑμῶν, ποιεῖτε
readings.en: what I have seen with my Father I speak; and you do what you have seen with your father
readings.plain: I speak of the things I have seen with my Father. You, in the same way, do the things you have seen with your father.

why: The older text is shorter and more open: it has no "my" or "your." The Plain takes the second half as a statement about the hearers' father and so supplies "your," which the Byzantine text writes out. "My" and "your" were probably added by copyists to make clear that two different fathers are meant, as 8:44 says; the second "seen" matches the first.

a: If you are Abraham's children, the works of Abraham are what you would be doing.
p: The Greek is a mixed condition; copyists smoothed it in two different ways.

readings.w: Papyrus 66 (corrected), 75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus (corrected), Bezae, W, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: Εἰ τέκνα τοῦ Ἀβραάμ ἐστε, τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ἐποιεῖτε
readings.en: if you are children of Abraham, you would be doing the works of Abraham
readings.plain: If you are Abraham's children, the works of Abraham are what you would be doing.

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "If ye were Abraham's children, ye would do the works of Abraham")
readings.orig: Εἰ τέκνα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ἦτε, τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ἐποιεῖτε [ἄν]
readings.en: if you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham
readings.plain: If you were Abraham's children, you would be doing the works of Abraham.

readings.w: Papyrus 66 (first hand), Vaticanus (first hand), as reported by Metzger; Westcott and Hort
readings.orig: Εἰ τέκνα τοῦ Ἀβραάμ ἐστε, τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ποιεῖτε
readings.en: if you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham
readings.plain: If you are Abraham's children, do the works of Abraham.

why: The mixed form ("if you are ... you would be doing") is awkward Greek, which explains both corrections: one makes the whole sentence contrary to fact, the other turns it into a command. The meaning is close in all three.

a: the one you say is 'our God.'
p: Manuscripts and editions divide between "our God" (direct speech) and "your God" (reported speech).

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Byzantine
readings.orig: ὃν ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι θεὸς ἡμῶν ἐστιν
readings.en: of whom you say, 'He is our God'
readings.plain: the one you say is 'our God.'

readings.w: THGNT, Westcott and Hort, Textus Receptus (KJV "of whom ye say, that he is your God")
readings.orig: ὃν ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι θεὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν
readings.en: of whom you say that he is your God
readings.plain: the one you say is your God.

why: The two Greek words differ by one letter and sounded alike in later Greek pronunciation, so copyists confused them easily, and Metzger reports that the manuscripts are closely divided. The Plain follows NA28 and SBL; the Tyndale House edition prefers "your." The meaning is the same.

a: and you have seen Abraham?
t: "You have seen Abraham" or "Abraham has seen you"?
p: A few early witnesses read "and Abraham has seen you?", which fits 8:56 more closely.

readings.w: Papyrus 66, Vaticanus, Bezae, W, most manuscripts, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: καὶ Ἀβραὰμ ἑώρακας;
readings.en: and you have seen Abraham?
readings.plain: and you have seen Abraham?

readings.w: Papyrus 75 (about 175–225), Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), 0124, the Sinaitic Syriac, the Sahidic Coptic, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: καὶ Ἀβραὰμ ἑώρακέν σε;
readings.en: and Abraham has seen you?
readings.plain: and Abraham has seen you?

why: The second reading has early witnesses and matches Jesus' words that Abraham saw his day (8:56). But that is exactly why a copyist might have changed it, and the first reading, where the hearers turn the claim around to mock it, has much wider support.

a: and he went out of the temple.
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add that Jesus went "through the midst of them, and so passed by."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ
readings.en: and went out of the temple
readings.plain: and he went out of the temple.

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "and went out of the temple, going through the midst of them, and so passed by")
readings.orig: καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ, διελθὼν διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν· καὶ παρῆγεν οὕτως
readings.en: and went out of the temple, passing through the middle of them, and so went on
readings.plain: and he went out of the temple, passing through the middle of them, and so he went on his way.

why: The addition is absent from the oldest manuscripts. It seems to borrow from Luke 4:30 ("passing through the middle of them, he went on his way") and from John 9:1 ("as he was passing by").

a: We have to do the works of the one who sent me
p: Manuscripts vary between "we ... sent me," "I ... sent me" and "we ... sent us."

readings.w: Papyrus 66 and 75, Vaticanus, Bezae, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ἡμᾶς δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι τὰ ἔργα τοῦ πέμψαντός με
readings.en: we must work the works of the one who sent me
readings.plain: We have to do the works of the one who sent me

readings.w: Sinaiticus (corrected), Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Θ, the Byzantine majority, as reported by Metzger; Textus Receptus (KJV "I must work the works of him that sent me")
readings.orig: ἐμὲ δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι τὰ ἔργα τοῦ πέμψαντός με
readings.en: I must work the works of the one who sent me
readings.plain: I have to do the works of the one who sent me

readings.w: Sinaiticus (first hand), L, W, the Sahidic Coptic, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: ἡμᾶς δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι τὰ ἔργα τοῦ πέμψαντος ἡμᾶς
readings.en: we must work the works of the one who sent us
readings.plain: We have to do the works of the one who sent us

why: "We ... sent me" is the most awkward form, and both others look like attempts to make the two pronouns agree. The "we" draws the disciples into Jesus' work.

a: as a beggar
p: The KJV says the neighbors had seen "that he was blind." The older manuscripts say "that he was a beggar."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ὅτι προσαίτης ἦν
readings.en: that he was a beggar
readings.plain: as a beggar

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "that he was blind")
readings.orig: ὅτι τυφλὸς ἦν
readings.en: that he was blind
readings.plain: as a blind man

why: "Beggar" has the stronger and older support and fits the next words, "the man who sat begging." "Blind" probably came in from the rest of the chapter.

a: the Son of Man
p: The KJV asks, "Dost thou believe on the Son of God?" The oldest manuscripts say "Son of Man."

readings.w: Papyrus 66 and 75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, W, the Sinaitic Syriac, the Coptic, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: εἰς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
readings.en: in the Son of Man
readings.plain: the Son of Man

readings.w: Alexandrinus, L, Θ, Ψ, the Byzantine majority, the Latin, Textus Receptus (KJV), as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: εἰς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ
readings.en: in the Son of God
readings.plain: the Son of God

why: The early evidence for "Son of Man" is strong and comes from many regions. A copyist could easily change it to "Son of God," the usual object of faith in Christian confessions (compare 20:31), but the reverse change is hard to explain. In John, the Son of Man is the one who judges (5:27), which fits 9:39.

a: He said, "I believe, Lord." And he bowed down and worshiped him.
p: Several early witnesses lack 9:38 and the opening of 9:39. This entry goes with the next one.

readings.w: Papyrus 66, Sinaiticus (corrected), Vaticanus, Bezae, nearly all later manuscripts, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: ὁ δὲ ἔφη· Πιστεύω, κύριε· καὶ προσεκύνησεν αὐτῷ.
readings.en: and he said, 'I believe, Lord,' and he worshiped him
readings.plain: He said, "I believe, Lord." And he bowed down and worshiped him.

readings.w: Papyrus 75 (about 175–225), Sinaiticus (first hand), W, the Old Latin manuscript b, a Coptic version, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: (9:38 and "And Jesus said" in 9:39 absent)
readings.en: the verse is not there

why: Most of the evidence includes the words, and the Plain follows it. Some scholars argue that the words were added from early baptism services, where a new believer confessed "I believe, Lord" and knelt; the unusual verb "he said" (ephē), rare in John, supports that view. Without them, Jesus' words in 9:37 run straight on into 9:39.

a: Jesus said,
p: Goes with the entry on 9:38: the same witnesses lack "And Jesus said."

readings.w: Papyrus 66, Vaticanus, most manuscripts, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
readings.en: and Jesus said
readings.plain: Jesus said,

readings.w: Papyrus 75, Sinaiticus (first hand), W, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: (absent)
readings.en: (Jesus continues speaking)

why: See the entry on 9:38.

a: I am the door for the sheep.
p: Papyrus 75 and the Sahidic Coptic read "I am the shepherd of the sheep."

readings.w: Papyrus 66, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, nearly all manuscripts, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα τῶν προβάτων
readings.en: I am the door of the sheep
readings.plain: I am the door for the sheep.

readings.w: Papyrus 75 (about 175–225), the Sahidic and Achmimic Coptic, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν τῶν προβάτων
readings.en: I am the shepherd of the sheep
readings.plain: I am the shepherd of the sheep.

why: "Door" is the harder image here, since 10:2 has just called the shepherd the one who comes through the door. A copyist or translator probably changed it to "shepherd" to smooth the figure, as 10:11 says.

a: Everyone who came before me
p: Some manuscripts, including the Byzantine majority, lack "before me"; the KJV's Textus Receptus has it.

readings.w: Papyrus 66, Sinaiticus (corrected), Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, Bezae, W, as reported by Metzger; NA28 (in brackets), SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "All that ever came before me")
readings.orig: πάντες ὅσοι ἦλθον πρὸ ἐμοῦ
readings.en: all who came before me
readings.plain: Everyone who came before me

readings.w: Papyrus 45 (probably) and 75, Sinaiticus (first hand), the Byzantine majority, much of the Latin and Syriac, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: πάντες ὅσοι ἦλθον
readings.en: all who came
readings.plain: Everyone who came

why: The evidence is divided. Without "before me," the saying is less likely to be read as condemning Moses and the prophets, and Metzger suggests some copyists dropped the words for that reason. The Plain follows the editions in keeping them; Jesus means false leaders, not the prophets (5:39, 46).

a: That is because he works for pay
p: The KJV starts the verse with "The hireling fleeth," from the Byzantine text, which repeats that the hired man runs.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ὅτι μισθωτός ἐστιν
readings.en: because he is a hired man
readings.plain: That is because he works for pay

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling")
readings.orig: ὁ δὲ μισθωτὸς φεύγει, ὅτι μισθωτός ἐστιν
readings.en: and the hired man runs away because he is a hired man
readings.plain: The hired man runs away because he works for pay

why: The shorter text carries on the sentence from 10:12, where the man has already run. The longer one repeats "runs away" so the verse can stand on its own, perhaps for public reading. The meaning is the same.

a: and those that are mine know me
t: "Mine know me" or "I am known by mine"?
p: The KJV's "and am known of mine" follows the Byzantine text.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: καὶ γινώσκουσί με τὰ ἐμά
readings.en: and mine know me
readings.plain: and those that are mine know me

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: καὶ γινώσκομαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν
readings.en: and I am known by mine
readings.plain: and I am known by those that are mine

why: The active form has much the older support. The passive is a stylistic change; the meaning is the same.

a: No one takes it away from me.
p: Some of the oldest manuscripts read "No one took it from me," as if looking back on the cross.

readings.w: Papyrus 66, Sinaiticus (corrected), Alexandrinus, Bezae, W, the Byzantine majority, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: οὐδεὶς αἴρει αὐτὴν ἀπ᾽ ἐμοῦ
readings.en: no one takes it from me
readings.plain: No one takes it away from me.

readings.w: Papyrus 45 (about 250), Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, as reported by Metzger; Westcott and Hort
readings.orig: οὐδεὶς ἦρεν αὐτὴν ἀπ᾽ ἐμοῦ
readings.en: no one took it from me
readings.plain: No one took it away from me.

why: The past tense has old witnesses and is the harder reading, and some scholars prefer it, hearing the voice of the risen Christ or of John's community. Most editions follow the present tense, which fits the present-tense verbs around it.

a: since you do not belong among my sheep.
p: The KJV adds "as I said unto you," which the oldest manuscripts lack.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ὅτι οὐκ ἐστὲ ἐκ τῶν προβάτων τῶν ἐμῶν
readings.en: because you are not of my sheep
readings.plain: since you do not belong among my sheep.

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: οὐ γάρ ἐστε ἐκ τῶν προβάτων τῶν ἐμῶν, καθὼς εἶπον ὑμῖν
readings.en: for you are not of my sheep, as I told you
readings.plain: since you do not belong among my sheep, as I told you.

why: Jesus has not said these words in so many words before, which may be why copyists added "as I told you" to the next sentence, or attached it here to point back to 10:1–16. The shorter text has the older support.

a: My Father, the one who gave them to me, is greater than all.
t: Who or what is "greater than all"?
p: The Greek of this verse comes in four forms. NA28 reads "What my Father has given me is greater than all."

readings.w: Papyrus 66, Θ, families 1 and 13, the Byzantine majority, as reported by Metzger; Textus Receptus (KJV "My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all")
readings.orig: ὁ πατήρ μου ὃς δέδωκέν μοι μείζων πάντων ἐστίν
readings.en: my Father, who has given (them) to me, is greater than all
readings.plain: My Father, the one who gave them to me, is greater than all.

readings.w: Sinaiticus, L, W, as reported by Metzger; SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ὁ πατήρ μου ὃ δέδωκέν μοι πάντων μείζων ἐστίν
readings.en: my Father, (as to) what he has given me, is greater than all
readings.plain: My Father, as for what he has given me, he is greater than all.

readings.w: Vaticanus (first hand), the Latin versions, as reported by Metzger; NA28
readings.orig: ὁ πατήρ μου ὃ δέδωκέν μοι πάντων μεῖζόν ἐστιν
readings.en: what my Father has given me is greater than all
readings.plain: What my Father has given me is greater than all.

readings.w: Alexandrinus, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: ὁ πατήρ μου ὃς δέδωκέν μοι πάντων μεῖζόν ἐστιν
readings.en: my Father, who has given (them) to me, (is) a greater thing than all
readings.plain: My Father, the one who gave them to me, is something greater than all.

why: The Plain renders the first reading, "who ... greater," and says so here. The SBL and Tyndale House text (the second reading) has a neuter "what" with a masculine "greater," a mix that is very hard to put into English; most translations of that text in practice read it as "who," so the sense matches the first reading, and the Father is the one who is greater. NA28's reading (the third) is the hardest and has good old support, and many scholars think it original: the flock the Father gave is precious beyond all, or held by a power greater than all. The fourth looks like a blend of the others. The next words, "no one can snatch them from the Father's hand," make sense on any of them.

a: Then you will come to know, and go on knowing,
p: The KJV's "that ye may know, and believe" follows the Byzantine text.

readings.w: Papyrus 45, 66 and 75, Vaticanus, L, W, Θ, as reported by Metzger; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ἵνα γνῶτε καὶ γινώσκητε
readings.en: so that you may know and keep on knowing
readings.plain: Then you will come to know, and go on knowing,

readings.w: Alexandrinus, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV), as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: ἵνα γνῶτε καὶ πιστεύσητε
readings.en: so that you may know and believe
readings.plain: Then you will come to know and believe

why: The repeated verb "know" (first a moment of recognition, then lasting knowledge) is unusual, and copyists replaced it with the more familiar pair "know and believe." The older papyri have the repetition.
